title: On‑Call Pocket Guide: Rapid Accelerator Substitute & Capacity Onramp (Draft)
body:
Purpose:
This pocket guide is a concise first-responder runbook for urgent accelerator (GPU/TPU) failures and short-term capacity shortfalls. It focuses on two complementary paths: (A) deploying a temporary substitute node to keep traffic flowing, and (B) fast onramp of capacity to restore steady-state throughput.

Scope and assumptions:
- Cluster: prod-rt (multi-az).
- Nodes are labeled with node.k8s.redwood/role=compute and accelerator tags (e.g., nvidia-a100, h100-q).
- We assume access to: kubectl context prod, redwoodctl (internal infra CLI), infra-terraform, and monitoring dashboards.
- This is a short-form operator checklist for oncall; deeper procedures live in Confluence (linked).

Immediate triage (first 5–10 min):
1) Observe: confirm impact level. Check dashboards: token-per-second, 99p latency, queue depth, and error-rate.
   - If user-facing degradation (>= 50% error or 2x latency) tag incident P1 and page SRE lead.
2) Identify failing host(s):
   - redwoodctl infra list-nodes --label accelerator --state=NotReady or kubectl get nodes -l node.k8s.redwood/role=compute -o wide
3) Gather quick facts: which model(s) affected, active pods on node, estimated reclaimable capacity.
4) Decide path: substitute node (fast) OR drain+replace (longer). Use substitute when: immediate SLA risk, node hardware fault requiring off-rack replacement, or cross-zone imbalance.

Path A — Rapid substitute node (hot-swap fallback):
Goal: attach a warm spare with compatible accelerator and shift subset of traffic to it with minimal disruption.
Steps:
- If spare pool exists (onramp/oncall-spares):
  1) Claim a spare: redwoodctl capacity claim --pool=onramp-spares --region=<az> --gpus=1
  2) Verify node is Ready and labeled: kubectl get nodes | grep <node-name> && kubectl label node <node-name> node.k8s.redwood/role=compute --overwrite
  3) Patch routing policy for gradual shift: redwoodctl route patch --model=<model> --from=<old-node> --to=<new-node> --strategy=gradual --pct=10
  4) Monitor model latency and error rates for 5–15m windows. Increase pct in steady increments (10 -> 30 -> 60 -> 100).
- If no spare: instantiate onramp (see Path B).
Notes:
- Keep KV cache restoration in mind: new node will be cold. Prefer moving non-latency-critical workloads first or use warm-caches when available.
- Mark the failed node: kubectl annotate node <failed-node> redwood.incident=<INC-ID>

Path B — Fast capacity onramp (when substitute isn't available):
Goal: add capacity quickly (spot or reserved) and rebalance traffic.
Steps (preferred order):
1) Prefer warm onramp pool: redwoodctl capacity add --pool=onramp-autoscale --gpus=2 --region=<az> --ttl=4h
2) If terraform is required (longer): cd infra/terraform/onramp && terraform apply -var region=<az> -auto-approve (only if approved by SRE lead)
3) After nodes are Ready, label them and add to scheduler pool: kubectl label node <name> node.k8s.redwood/role=compute, kubectl annotate node <name> accelerator-ready=true
4) Kick off controlled routing: redwoodctl route set --model=<model> --pool=onramp-autoscale --strategy=canary --batch=5
5) Monitor metrics; keep a close eye on token-tail latency.

Cordon and drain checklist (safe removal of a degraded node):
- Use when node needs hardware replacement or planned reboot.
1) Cordon: kubectl cordon <node>  # prevents new pods
2) Drain: kubectl drain <node> --ignore-daemonsets --delete-emptydir-data --force --grace-period=120 --timeout=900s
3) Verify pods evicted and restarted elsewhere: kubectl get pods -o wide --field-selector spec.nodeName!=<node> -l model=serving
4) If pods stuck: describe pod and check events (image pull, PVC mount). If PVC lock prevents eviction, coordinate with storage SRE.
5) Once drained, mark node for maintenance: redwoodctl infra mark-maintenance <node> --reason="hw-fault" --inc=<INC-ID>

Hardware replacement quick notes (for on-site or lab tech):
- If board-level swap required, use accelerator service ticket template (link in linked_artifacts).
- For hot-swap capable chassis: follow hardware vendor checklist: power-cycle host -> reseat GPU in same riser -> vendor diagnostics -> bring node back to service.

Cluster recovery & rebalance (post-fix):
- After new capacity is added or node repaired:
  1) Run a small fleet-level rebalance: redwoodctl scheduler rebalance --selector node.k8s.redwood/role=compute --concurrency=10
  2) Warm caches: run synthetic prompt sets via redwoodctl perf replay --target-pool=<new-nodes> --dataset=prod-warm-keys --concurrency=20
  3) Run smoke tests for top 3 models, validate latencies and correctness.

Decision guide (quick):
- Symptom: single node transient NotReady (<10min) -> monitor 10–15m; auto-recover likely.
- Symptom: NotReady >15m with hardware errors -> cordon & drain -> Substitute OR onramp.
- Capacity shortfall (sustained CPU/GPU saturation >85% for 10+ min) -> onramp and temporary routing throttles to non-critical customers.

Escalation and comms:
- Page SRE lead if impact >= P1. Include: incident ID, affected models, current qps and 99p latency, mitigation in progress.
- Post updates every 15–30m in incident channel. Use template: "[INC-xxxx] current state — mitigation step — next check-in in 15m".
- If customer-facing degradation, coordinate with CS to draft customer message.

Quick commands cheat-sheet:
- kubectl cordon <node>
- kubectl drain <node> --ignore-daemonsets --delete-emptydir-data --force
- kubectl get pods -o wide --field-selector spec.nodeName=<node>
- redwoodctl infra list-nodes --state=NotReady
- redwoodctl capacity claim --pool=onramp-spares --gpus=1 --region=<az>
- redwoodctl capacity add --pool=onramp-autoscale --gpus=2 --region=<az>
- redwoodctl route patch --model=<model> --to=<node> --strategy=gradual --pct=10
- rwinfctl cache prewarm --nodes=<node-list> --dataset=prod-warm-keys

Playbook pitfalls and tips:
- Avoid moving 100% traffic to a cold node at once — KV cache miss will spike latency.
- If using spot instances for onramp, add fallback routing to dedicated pool early.
- Label hygiene: double-check labels after Terraform/auto-scaling boot — missing labels = scheduler ignores node.
- Timebox actions: if substitute path isn't steady after 30 minutes, escalate and consider permanent replacement.

Post-incident template (to fill after stabilization):
- Incident ID:
- Start / End times:
- Impact summary (models, % requests affected):
- Action path taken (A or B) and why:
- Commands run (copy/paste):
- Root cause hypothesis / confirmed cause:
- Follow-ups / owners (replace HW, improve warm-pool size, add alert rule):
- Lessons learned (what to change in this doc):

Appendix: useful links
- Accelerator lifecycle Confluence (linked)
- Infra tools PR for automated claim flow (linked)
- Incident template and customer comms draft (confluence/CS docs)

Notes to self (work-in-progress):
- Investigate automated prewarm: choreography between routing service and cache prewarm API.
- Consider metric: "fraction of traffic routed to cold nodes" -> alert when > 0.2 for 10m.
- Add a small synthetic test that runs immediately after any new node Ready event.

End of pocket guide (draft).
